# Puzzle

## The puzzle

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
> "The best industrial policy is to have no industrial policy."
> --- Pedro Malan, Minister of Finance

\vspace{1em}

Yet the government **sponsored** the mergers that built two national champions: Gerdau and Ambev.

**How pursue industrial policy while denying it?** Not through subsidies or protection, but by **reinterpreting the enforcement of competition law** --- at no cost to the Treasury.
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
![Pedro Malan, Minister of Finance](figures/malan.jpg){width=90%}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Read the Malan quote aloud --- it is a gift, so let it land before you say anything. Then turn it: the very government that said this personally sponsored the mergers that built Gerdau and Ambev. Put the question on the table and leave it hanging --- how do you run an industrial policy while denying the category exists?

Shape the answer without giving it away: not by spending, because there was no money --- this is a government in fiscal crisis --- but through how it enforced competition law. "At no cost to the Treasury" is the thread that runs through the entire talk; say it here so the audience is listening for it. The face on the slide is the man who denied the category.
:::

## The argument

**Antitrust can serve as a *passive, fiscally cheap* industrial policy** --- we study a case of a fiscally conservative, liberalizing government that explicitly denies doing industrial policy.

\vfill

- **Claim.** Brazil's flexible antitrust enforcement in the 1990s worked as *de facto* industrial policy, forging "national champions" to become brazillian multinational companies.
- **Evidence.** Two government-backed mergers: **Gerdau/Pains** (steel) and **Antarctica--Brahma → Ambev** (beer).
- **Mechanism.** **Institutional conversion** (Mahoney & Thelen 2010) of a young competition regime --- against its original intent.

::: {.notes}
State the claim in a single breath and do not over-explain it --- explaining it is the rest of the talk. The one counter-intuitive claim: a government that publicly swore off industrial policy ran one anyway, through its competition authority. Name the two cases --- steel and beer --- as the evidence, and name the mechanism, institutional conversion, but promise to unpack it rather than unpacking it here.

The hook to plant, and it is what makes the paper fun: nothing in this story is illegal, and almost nothing is even hidden. The statute never changes a word --- only its reading does. Keep it to about forty-five seconds; this slide is a promise, and the promise is that we go to the cases fast.
:::

# The problem

## The received view --- and its crack

- Antitrust scholarship, from **Brandeis to Williamson**, rejects state-led industrial policy as market-distorting.
- Yet early-20th-century U.S. market regulation already worked as *de facto* industrial policy, without direct state intervention (Dobbin 1994; Prasad 2012).

\vfill

**The antitrust / industrial-policy boundary was always porous.** The question is *how* the crossing happens in a liberalizing context.

::: {.notes}
Set up the opposition in everyday terms before naming any school. For a century these were understood as opposite jobs. Antitrust is the referee: it does not care who wins, only that nobody rigs the game. Industrial policy is the coach: it deliberately picks a team and helps it win. On the received view a state does one or the other.

The crack: Dobbin and Prasad showed that the referee's rulebook was never neutral. Which industries grew in the early United States depended on how the rules of market competition were written and enforced --- no ministry of industry required. So the referee was quietly coaching all along.

That is all this slide needs to establish. We are not claiming the boundary is fake; we are claiming it is porous, and asking how a government crosses it when it is publicly committed to not crossing it.
:::

## Economization: form-based vs. effect-based

Ergen & Kohl (2019): since the 1960s, competition regimes were **economized** --- reoriented from broad societal goals to economic ones --- in two opposed forms.

\vspace{0.4em}
\footnotesize

| | **Form-based** (Ordoliberal) | **Effect-based** (Chicago) |
|---|---|---|
| Illegality | Of certain structures *per se* | Only if net harm is shown |
| Tools | Structural presumptions, thresholds | Rule of reason, efficiency defense |
| Remedies | Structural (divestiture) | Behavioral (conduct) |
| Discretion | **One** soft joint: market definition | **Three**: market, effects, efficiencies |

\normalsize

The two concepts bent in Brazil --- **efficiency** and **relevant market** --- are exactly the joints the effect-based approach pries open.

::: {.notes}
This is the one piece of theory the cases need --- give it, then get to the cases. Do not linger.

Start with what competition law was originally *for*. When these laws were written, the worry was not mainly about prices; it was that concentrated private power is dangerous to a democracy. Those were broad social goals. "Economization" is Ergen and Kohl's name for what happened from the 1960s on: regulators quietly dropped the social goals and kept only economic ones.

The analogy that lands with a lay audience is traffic enforcement. Form-based is a posted speed limit: over the line is illegal, full stop. Effect-based asks instead, "was your driving actually dangerous?" --- and now you get to argue: empty road, clear weather, skilled driver. Both are real ways to regulate. But only the second requires somebody to make a judgment call in every single case.

The payoff is the bottom row, and it is the one thing to carry into the cases. Every judgment call is a place a decision could have gone either way --- a discretionary joint. Form-based has roughly one: where you draw the market. Effect-based has three: the market, the predicted effects, and whether the claimed efficiencies count. More joints, more room for pressure to enter *without anyone breaking a rule*. That single idea is what will explain why Gerdau was a public brawl and Ambev was quiet.
:::

# Context

## From military developmentalism to the regulatory state

- **The military state (1964--85):** national-developmentalism --- import substitution, state-owned firms, market reserves, tariff walls.
- **FHC's rupture (1995--2002):** trade opening, **privatization** (Vale 1997, Telebrás 1998), the end of market reserves, fiscal discipline.
- **A new bureaucracy** --- Bresser-Pereira's *managerial reform* (MARE / PDRAE, 1995): from a patrimonial-bureaucratic state to a **regulatory** one, staffed by technocrats and independent agencies (ANEEL, ANATEL, ANP).
- **CADE (strengthened 1994) is a child of this moment:** a technocratic regulator born as the state stopped *producing* and started *regulating*.

\vfill

**Liberalization *reconfigured* state power --- it did not retreat.** The same move that built the regulatory state built the discretion antitrust would convert.

::: {.notes}
This slide exists to kill a misreading. People hear "1990s liberalisation in Latin America" and picture the state shrinking and walking off the field. That picture is wrong, and our argument depends on it being wrong.

Cardoso broke with the military model --- import substitution, state firms, market reserves --- but he did not abolish the state; he changed its job. Bresser-Pereira's reform rebuilt the bureaucracy into a regulatory one: independent agencies, technocrats, rules. CADE is a child of exactly that impulse.

Land the closing line and let it carry: liberalisation reconfigured state power, it did not retreat --- and the very discretion the new regulatory state manufactured is what antitrust would later convert. The state did not leave; it changed weapons. If you are short on time, this is a slide you can move through quickly.
:::

## Context: liberalization and runaway inflation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Liberalization followed decades of direct intervention: state-owned firms, protectionism, price controls and trusts.
- In a period of **runaway inflation**, stabilization (the Real Plan) made **competition a tool of inflation control** --- not a developmental one.
- Trade opening exposed domestic firms, raising fears of **denationalization**.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Price-tagging amid runaway inflation](figures/price-gun-tomato-extract.jpg){width=100%}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Two facts, held in tension. One: the overriding priority was killing inflation --- the Real Plan --- so competition policy arrived wearing an anti-inflation uniform, not a developmental one. Nobody set CADE up to build champions; it was there to keep prices down. Two: trade opening frightened domestic firms, because foreigners could now walk in and buy them --- the spectre of denationalisation.

So you have an agency designed to discipline the market, operating in a climate terrified of losing its firms to foreigners. Our whole story happens in the gap between those two facts. The photograph is the inflation everyone was desperate to leave behind.
:::

## A new competition authority (1994)

- The 1994 law granted autonomy to **CADE** (Administrative Council for Economic Defense); councilors appointed by the President.
- Mandate: "strengthen the competition culture" --- competition **as part of inflation control**.

\vfill

**CADE's challenge:** to legitimate a brand-new mandate --- a young regime with **no entrenched professional community** to defend it.

::: {.notes}
One structural detail here does a lot of work later, so flag it now: CADE became autonomous in 1994, but the President appoints its councillors. Hold that thought for when Cardoso swaps them mid-case. Its official mission was to build a "competition culture" as part of holding inflation down.

But the line to stress is the last one --- this was a two-year-old agency with no professional community behind it. In Germany a century of ordoliberal lawyers stood ready to defend the doctrine; in Brazil there was nobody yet. That empty container --- discretion with nothing to discipline it --- is the point we cash out at the very end.
:::

# Gerdau--Pains

## The rebars of discord

- Gerdau acquires Korf's Brazilian assets; the vertical-integration part is approved unanimously.
- Contention centers on the **steel rebar market** (Korf's core business), where Gerdau's share would approach **50%**.
- Under Law 8.884/94, a **20% structural threshold** still bit --- a hard, *form-based* element.

::: {.notes}
First case, and keep it physical. Gerdau bought Korf's Brazilian assets; the vertical part was uncontroversial and waved through. The whole fight is about one product --- rebar, the steel rods in every building site --- where Gerdau would reach nearly half the market.

Plant the one technical fact that matters: the 1994 law still carried a hard number, a twenty-per-cent structural threshold. That is a form-based fossil sitting inside the new regime, and it is about to force an open confrontation. Foreshadow it: because that number is rigid, argument alone will not move it. Remember that when Ambev, which had no such number in play, goes quietly.
:::

## Gerdau--Pains: timeline

- **Mar 1995** --- CADE postpones; the deal would lift Gerdau's long-steel share **39.6% → 46.2%**.
- **Oct 1995** --- **partial approval, deconstitution ordered** (46.5% of common long steel; the law bars >20%).
- **Late 1995** --- refusing compliance, Gerdau bypasses the courts and appeals to Justice Minister **Jobim**, who suspends the ruling --- *contra* Art. 50 ("no executive review").
- **Then** --- Cardoso **recomposes CADE**, replacing jurists with transaction-cost economists ("Don't cause me problems!").
- **Mar 1998** --- the reconfigured CADE approves with **10 conditions**: keep Pains, but sell the Contagem rolling unit and Transpains, rehire workers, invest US\$78M.
- **1999** --- the champion goes global: 75% of **AmeriSteel** (US).

::: {.notes}
Do not read the dates --- narrate the arc. CADE looks at the numbers and says no: partial approval, undo the concentrating part. Gerdau then does something remarkable --- instead of going to court, it goes to the Justice Minister, who suspends CADE's decision, even though the law says in black and white that the executive cannot review CADE. Then the councillors who said no are replaced. And only in 1998, three years on, does a reshaped CADE approve the deal, with ten conditions.

End on the payoff: the champion immediately goes global, buying into the United States the very next year. The point is not the chronology --- it is that winning this one required overriding the law's own rule and changing the referees. That is the expensive, ugly way to convert a regime. Ambev will show the cheap way.
:::

## Gerdau: why it took brute force

- **Relevant market** --- firms: steel is a *global commodity*. CADE: domestic prices **decoupled** from world benchmarks → national market.
- **Efficiency (Art. 54)** --- firms: proprietary technology, rescue of distressed assets. CADE: achievable **without** integration; no consumer gain.

\vfill

**Only one soft joint (market definition)** → the executive had to act *against the letter of the law* (Jobim) and **replace the councilors** with transaction-cost economists ("Don't cause me problems!" --- Cardoso).

::: {.notes}
Cash in the theory here. The 1994 law still had one hard, form-based number in it: twenty per cent. Gerdau would be at forty-six and a half. There is nothing to weigh, nothing to balance --- the number simply decides. So the only thing left to argue about was the one soft joint: where you draw the boundary of "the market."

Explain that move concretely, because it is the single most useful thing a lay audience can take away. If the market is "steel sold in Brazil," Gerdau is enormous. If the market is "steel in the world," Gerdau is a minor player. Same company, same mills, same customers --- the answer flips entirely depending on where you draw the line. That is why the fight was about market definition, and why the minister's order was about exactly that: declaring the Brazilian steel market open to international products.

CADE's counter was empirical and it held: domestic prices had come loose from world benchmarks, so in practice this was a national market. The firms lost the argument on the merits.

Hence the punchline. With only one joint to work, argument was not enough --- the outcome required a minister to override a decision the law said he could not review, and then required replacing the people who made it. Brute force, in public. Remember this when we get to Ambev, where none of that was necessary.
:::

# Ambev

## The "green-and-yellow multinational"

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- After failed tie-ups with foreign firms, the two largest brewers --- **Antarctica and Brahma** --- merge into **Ambev** (1999).
- Framed as a *verde-e-amarela* champion; executives mobilized fears of **denationalization**.
- Costly domestic credit let foreign rivals **outbid** Brazilian firms --- scale at home as a defense.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Ambev: "the flavor of Brazil to the world"](figures/ambev-flavor-of-brazil.png){width=100%}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Set beer up as more than beer. Through the 1990s the global brewers circled Antarctica and Brahma; the founders' fear --- and their ambition --- was denationalisation. So they fused the two largest domestic brewers into a self-declared "green-and-yellow multinational," a national champion in so many words.

Draw out the fiscal twist, because it ties straight to our thesis: domestic credit was so expensive that a foreign buyer could always outbid a Brazilian one, so building scale at home was the only affordable defence. That is why the state's help had to be non-fiscal --- nobody had cheap money to hand out. The video still is the champion selling itself, literally, as Brazil to the world.
:::

## Ambev: a public war

- **Jul 1999** --- unveiled at the **Palácio da Alvorada**, Cardoso beside the founders; the new firm holds **~70%** of beer.
- **14 Jul** --- CADE strikes back with a **precautionary suspension** --- yet the firms already operate as one, a *fait accompli*.
- **Media war** --- rival **Kaiser** runs **three** press campaigns: "the merger means higher prices, against the consumer."
- **The staff revolt** --- SEAE finds efficiencies of **6.9%**, not the claimed 14.1%; a **Federal Police bribery probe** brushes the council.
- **The executive leans in** --- ministers phone CADE's president; Dev. Minister Carvalho dangles **R\$3bn** of BNDES for champions; Cardoso: "the world runs on oligopoly."
- **Mar 2000** --- approved over **one dissent** (Ruy Lima) --- a Performance Commitment Term: sell the weak *Bavária*, keep *Skol*.

::: {.notes}
Perform this slide --- do not summarise it. The audience should feel that this was a real public brawl, because the payoff on the next slide depends on the contrast.

The merger is announced not in a boardroom but at the presidential palace, with Cardoso standing between the two founders. CADE slaps a precautionary suspension on it --- but the companies are already running as a single firm, essentially daring the agency to unscramble the egg. The rival Kaiser takes the fight to the public with three separate advertising campaigns. The agency's own technical staff revolt: the promised efficiency gains collapse from fourteen per cent to under seven, and a Federal Police bribery investigation brushes the council. Meanwhile ministers are phoning CADE's president, the development minister is openly offering three billion reais of state-bank money to build champions, and the President is on record that the world runs on oligopoly. One councillor, Ruy Lima, votes no. It passes anyway.

Hold the paradox --- resolve it on the next slide, not here. This was a far bigger, louder war than Gerdau, and yet nobody had to break a law, override a ruling, or replace anyone. That contrast is the whole argument, and it lands hardest if you let this slide be loud and the next one quiet.

On the bribery probe: state it as a fact --- an investigation touched the council --- and move on. Do not insinuate a verdict; our claim does not rest on corruption, and saying so out loud pre-empts the question.
:::

## Ambev: the effect-based regime at work

- **Relevant market** --- Ambev: define broadly as *"beverages"*, frame rivalry as international (vs. Coca-Cola). Critics/SEAE: the market is **beer**, exports **<1%**.
- **Efficiency** --- **14.1%** claimed vs. **6.9%** found; speculative, unlikely to reach consumers.
- **CADE (Gesner Oliveira):** regulate **conduct over structure** → approved with conditions.

\vfill

An even louder war than Gerdau --- media, ministers, a bribery probe, a lone dissent --- and **yet no illegal override**. The three joints had room; the doctrine absorbed it.

::: {.notes}
Walk the three joints in order, so the audience sees the machine from the economization slide actually running.

Joint one, the market. Ambev argued the relevant market was "beverages" and the real rivalry was global, against Coca-Cola. Critics answered: the market is beer, and exports were under one per cent. Same trick attempted as in Gerdau --- but now it is one argument among three rather than the whole battlefield.

Joint two, the effects. Ambev claimed efficiency gains of fourteen point one per cent; the technical bodies found six point nine. Note what has happened: we are now arguing about a *forecast*. Nobody can check it, because the merger has not happened yet. That is not a flaw in anyone's competence --- it is what asking about effects requires.

Joint three, whether those gains count. Even the six point nine was judged speculative and unlikely to reach consumers. And yet the merger was approved, with behavioural conditions rather than structural ones.

Now the comparison, which is the whole point of pairing these cases. The political pressure was at least as heavy as in Gerdau --- the merger was announced at the presidential palace. But nothing illegal happened. No minister overrode anything. No one was replaced. The reasoning simply absorbed it. That is what institutional conversion looks like from the inside: the statute never changed a word, and the outcome changed completely.

If someone asks whether the councillors were corrupt or captured, resist that framing. Our claim is about available doctrine, not about bad faith. A regime with three discretionary joints can reach this outcome with everyone acting in good faith. That is what makes it worth studying.
:::

# Discussion

## Discussion: the two cases compared

- **Gerdau (form-based, still hard):** one discretionary joint → open conflict and an *illegal* override.
- **Ambev (effect-based, installed):** three joints → the same pressure absorbed as routine.
- The sequence measures **how many discretionary joints the regime had** --- not actor fatigue.
- **Conversion = a fiscally free industrial policy** (forbearance, not spending): "passive."
- **Denial = illegibility.**
- **Caveat (Ergen & Kohl):** change is *piecemeal*; two cases are a precedent, not a permanent regime.

::: {.notes}
This is the hinge: the two cases went opposite ways, and the reason is the one idea from the economization slide. Gerdau had a hard threshold and one soft joint, so it took brute, illegal force. Ambev had three soft joints, so identical pressure was absorbed with nobody breaking a rule. The difference is not that the actors tired; it is how much room the doctrine gave them.

State the caveat yourself rather than waiting for it from the floor. Ergen and Kohl insist that this kind of change happens piece by piece, never by one comprehensive reform. That cuts against us: two cases establish a repertoire that was *available*, not a regime permanently installed. Concede it cleanly --- it costs nothing and buys credibility for everything else.

Two follow-ups worth having ready. Business power: Kaiser ran three campaigns against the merger, so Brazilian business was divided --- business pressure alone cannot explain the outcome; the state taking one faction's side does. Durability: Bouças notes CADE re-tightened its rules in the 2000s, so whether the conversion persisted is an open question we flag rather than settle.
:::

## Brazil's contribution: policy under public denial

- **Public denial is the crux.** Industrial policy pursued while disavowed at the programmatic level (Malan) --- not merely quiet, but officially rejected.
- **Denial → illegibility.** The developmental aim leaves no trace in the doctrine; it survives only in the case files --- so **process tracing** is the necessary method, not a convenience.
- **Conversion → fiscally free.** The champion is forged by *forbearance* (letting firms concentrate), not by spending. That is what "*passive*" means.
- **The irony.** The effects-based toolkit was built (Chicago) to keep the state *out*; in Brazil it let the state *in*. Conversion runs on **loud executive politics + personnel turnover** --- "covert" is *constitutive*, not cosmetic.

::: {.notes}
This is where we say what is ours. Four beats, and the last one is the one people remember.

On denial: this is not a government being discreet. Malan publicly rejected the whole category of industrial policy. That is stronger than staying quiet, and it is the condition everything else follows from.

On illegibility: if you read CADE's decisions cold, they look like ordinary competition law about consumer welfare. The developmental purpose is simply not in the text. That is why we trace the process through case files, press and testimony --- the method is forced on us by the object.

On "passive": no money changed hands. The state built a champion by *not* blocking a merger. For a government under fiscal discipline, that is the cheapest industrial policy there is --- which is exactly why it was available when subsidies were not.

Then the irony, and let it breathe. The flexible case-by-case toolkit was invented in Chicago by people whose declared purpose was keeping government out of the economy. Transplanted into Brazil, that same toolkit is precisely what let the government in. Same instrument, opposite politics. Ergen and Kohl document the German ordoliberals blocking that flexibility in the 1970s because they feared it would become industrial policy. Brazil is what they were afraid of.
:::

## Industrial policy: the normality of denial

> "Government policies that **explicitly target the transformation of the structure of economic activity** in pursuit of some public goal. ... A key characteristic is the exercise of **choice and discretion** by the public authorities --- '*We promote X but not Y*' --- though the latter part is **typically left implicit**." (Juhász, Lane & Rodrik 2024)

\vfill

- **Not fiscal by definition:** "the gamut runs from import protection to **exemptions from specific regulations**" --- industrial policy can run through the regulatory apparatus, at no Treasury cost.
- **Discretion and denial are built in:** the selective "X but not Y" is "typically left implicit"; in developing countries the term itself is avoided for its "negative connotation."
- **Brazil is not a freak --- it is the pure case:** the *targeting* is deliberate; only the *label* is denied.

::: {.notes}
Having shown the mechanism in two cases, widen out and pre-empt the "isn't this just Brazil being Brazil?" reaction. Juhász, Lane and Rodrik --- the current authority on industrial policy --- define it in a way that makes our case the normal case, not the exception.

Two moves. First, their definition is about goals, not tools: no subsidy required, "the gamut runs from import protection to exemptions from specific regulations." That is exactly what lets antitrust count. Second, and this is the sentence to land: the selective favouring is "typically left implicit," and in developing countries the term itself is avoided for its "negative connotation." The leading industrial-policy economists are telling you that denial is normal. Brazil is just the pure form of it. Pre-empt one objection: "explicitly target" does not mean publicly announced --- it means deliberately selective.
:::

## Three fates of administrative discretion

Foster & Thelen (2024): the **administrative-law structure** --- how much discretion regulators hold, and *how it is disciplined* --- decides which paradigm sticks. Ergen & Kohl supply the ideas; the container decides their fate.

\vspace{0.4em}
\footnotesize

| Regime | Discretion disciplined by | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **Germany** | Ordoliberal **rules** (form-based profession) | Robust form-based control; blocks economization |
| **EU** | **Social learning** (deliberative administration) | Brandeisian *"regulated competition"* |
| **Brazil** | **Nothing yet** --- young regime, executive capture | **Conversion** → covert industrial policy |

\normalsize

\vfill

**Discretion is not destiny --- the *container* decides.** Brazil fills the missing cell: discretion captured *before* a profession could discipline it.

::: {.notes}
This is the closing widen-out: from our two Brazilian cases to how antitrust works across the world. Recall the economization idea --- which *ideas* win. This slide is about the *container* those ideas land in. Foster and Thelen present themselves as the complement to Ergen and Kohl: they cite them by name and say --- you showed which ideas won, we show what determines whether an idea can be put into practice.

Their variable in plain language is discretion: how much room the regulator has, and who can overrule it. In the United States, judges constantly substitute their judgment for the agency's, so it stops experimenting. In the European Union the Commission decides directly and courts defer on economics, so it can try things and adjust --- "social learning." Germany disciplined discretion with rules and stayed form-based; the EU disciplined it with learning and became Brandeisian; Brazil had the discretion and nothing to discipline it. Same lever, three outcomes --- Brazil is the cell their table was missing.

Two honesties for the floor. First, Foster and Thelen think discretion is a *good* thing --- our case is the other face of the same coin: the room that lets a regulator learn also lets an executive lean. Second, present the container as an *enabling condition*, not a cause --- Germany nearly went the other way in 1967, so it was a professional fight, not structure, that decided. Brazil's row is a claim we illustrate, not a variable we have measured.
:::
